name: Government & regulators
description: Provincial and federal bodies that issue mineral rights and permits, run environmental assessment, hold the Crown's duty to consult, and set policy. Courts sit here too because they define what the Crown owes.

name: Indigenous rights holders & organizations
description: First Nations and the Red River Métis hold constitutionally protected rights that trigger the Crown's duty to consult. Political organizations speak for groups of Nations. Several Nations are also project owners or partners, so this category overlaps with industry and with local communities.

name: Industry
description: Companies that hold mineral tenure and carry projects from staking to closure, plus their associations and contractors. Size and stage matter: majors operate mines, juniors explore and usually sell or option their discoveries.

name: Money & finance
description: Capital markets, tax-advantaged flow-through investors, public funds, private investors and royalty holders. Who pays, and on what timetable, shapes when engagement happens and how much time it gets.

name: Communities & civil society
description: Host municipalities, residents' groups, environmental organizations, labour and business groups. Many First Nations are also local communities; they are listed under Indigenous rights holders because their legal position differs.

name: Professional services & knowledge
description: Consultants who write assessments and run engagement, lawyers, and universities. They rarely decide, but they often frame what decision-makers see.

name: Markets & infrastructure
description: Buyers of concentrate, metal, sand and glass, and the power, rail and port infrastructure that a mine needs. Offtake agreements and grid access can decide whether a project is financeable.
